title: Write a field value the way its format says

blocks.text: Every data element has a format, written the way the data element tables write it: `n6`, `an12`, `n..19`, `ans..999`. The format is all a receiver has to find where one field ends and the next begins, so a value written in any other shape breaks the rest of the message.
Write `FieldEncoder.encode(String format, String value)`, which returns the field as it goes on the wire.

items: The format is a type followed by either a length (`n6`: fixed, exactly 6 characters) or `..` and a maximum (`n..19`: variable, up to 19).

The types are `n` (digits), `a` (letters), `an` (letters and digits), `ans` (any printable ASCII character, space included) and `z` (track 2: digits and `=`). A value with a character outside its type is refused.
A fixed field is padded to its full length. Numeric fields are padded with zeros on the left; every other type with spaces on the right.
A variable field is not padded. It is preceded by its length, written with as many digits as the maximum has: two for `n..19` or `ans..40`, three for `ans..999`.
A value longer than the field allows is refused.

blocks.text: Refuse with an `IllegalArgumentException`. You may assume the format itself is well formed.

cases.says: pads a fixed field to its width, prefixes a variable field with its length, and refuses characters outside the field's type
a short numeric value is padded on the left with zeros, so the number does not change
a value longer than its field allows is refused, never cut short

concepts: A fixed-length field always occupies its full width, so a shorter value is padded with a filler character.
A field's format, such as n6, an12 or ans..40, names its data type, whether it is fixed or variable, and its length or maximum.
A variable-length field is written as a fixed-width length indicator followed by exactly that many characters.
